transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-03 14:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jesse (Redwood AE), Anika (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya Chen (Skyforge Head of ML), Carlos (Platform), Lena (CTO)

[00:00] Jesse: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros. I'm Jesse Park, AE at Redwood, and Anika's our SE who will run the bench.
[00:08] Maya: Hi, Maya Chen, head of ML at Skyforge. we're doing a POC to validate latency/cost tradeoffs for our new genomics assistant.
[00:14] Carlos: Carlos Ruiz, platform eng, I'll handle networking and infra questions.
[00:18] Lena: Lena Vogel, CTO. high level: we need predictable latency and strong audit logs for compliance.
[00:25] Jesse: Great. objective today is to scope capacity for a 6-week POC — reserved GPUs with burst capacity — and figure out success criteria and fallback behavior.
[00:35] Anika: Quick agenda: workload description, traffic profile, target SLOs, bench plan, and then operational fallback + cost.

[01:05] Maya: Our workload is twofold: an interactive assistant for researchers (short to medium prompts, 50-600 tokens typical) and a nightly batch annotator job — big sequences up to 4k tokens, but lower concurrency. The interactive is latency sensitive, batch is throughput sensitive.

[01:40] Jesse: Can you quantify concurrency? p95 or p99 token/req?
[01:45] Maya: For interactive — typically 30 to 80 concurrent users during daytime peaks. median request is ~120 tokens, p95 token lengths around 480. For batch we run 2000 sequences overnight, each about 2k tokens.
[02:05] Carlos: On infra, we currently run model serving on an internal k8s cluster with Triton for some models, but it's fairly brittle. We're open to Redwood Dedicated or Private; initial POC prefers dedicated reserved pool in us-west with VPC peering.
[02:26] Anika: Sounds good. For POC we usually provision a reserved GPU pool sized to meet interactive p95 latency SLO, with a burst buffer that can spin up additional capacity. We'll also define fallbacks to a smaller quantized model to avoid request drops.

[03:00] Jesse: What are your latency targets?
[03:03] Lena: For interactive, we want p95 < 600ms for short prompts and p95 < 1s for up to 600 tokens. Batch can take longer — throughput matters more.
[03:16] Maya: Also need 99th percentile for interactive to be < 2s, else researcher experience degrades.

[03:40] Anika: Okay. Operational approach I'd recommend: 1) Reserved pool sized to handle baseline concurrency (say 80 users, typical token distributions) with continuous batching tuned for low latency; 2) Burst capacity that uses pre-warmed instances for fast scale up to handle spikes; 3) Fallback policy chain: primary full-precision model -> smaller quantized variant -> best-effort queued processing. We can also route to a lower-cost region if latency tradeoff acceptable.

[04:25] Carlos: How fast does burst warm up? we can't have researchers seeing long stalls while GPUs spin up.
[04:31] Anika: Pre-warmed burst nodes are recommended. warm-up can be sub 30s for pre-warmed GPUs, but cold start for a new instance could be 2-4 minutes depending on image and model load. We'll size pre-warm to cover typical spike envelope.

[05:00] Jesse: Let's walk through a sizing calc live. You said 80 concurrent interactive users, median 120 tokens per request, average generation maybe 150 tokens produced. What's your tokens/sec per user expectation?
[05:14] Maya: Roughly 20 tokens/sec per user on average requests when model is generating — varies. sometimes researchers ask longer chain-of-thought prompts, but average is around 15-25.
[05:29] Anika: If we assume 20 tokens/sec and average 150 generated tokens, that's ~7.5s of generation per request, but continuous batching on the runtime and KV cache for follow-ups will reduce end-to-end. For latency SLOs we'll tune prompt truncation and early-stopping heuristics too.

[06:05] Anika: For GPU sizing, comparisons: on an A100-80GB-style instance (or equivalent), we can serve roughly X concurrent streams for your model family depending on quantization. For baseline planning I'd propose reserving 4 GPUs for interactive baseline and 2 GPUs for batch workers, with a burst pool of 6 GPUs pre-warmed for spikes. That gives headroom for 80 concurrent interactive sessions and overnight batch throughput.

[06:40] Maya: Is that 4 GPUs enough for p95 < 600ms?
[06:43] Anika: Likely yes assuming int8 quantized model for most requests and optimized kernel paths, but we'll validate in bench. If we need lower latency, we can increase reserved to 6 and reduce burst. The bench will give the precise concurrency numbers.

[07:05] Jesse: On fallback policy specifics — customers often ask whether we fall back by truncation, switch to a distilled model, or queue. Which do you prefer?
[07:13] Maya: We want graceful degradation: prefer to switch to a distilled / quantized model that maintains quality, then queue if that fails. Truncation is undesirable for many research prompts.

[07:30] Anika: Agreed. For the POC we'll prepare two model variants: full fp16 (quality baseline) and int8-distilled variant that is ~2-3x faster with slightly lower quality. We'll define automatic routing rules by load and per-request SLO breach.

[08:00] Carlos: About data controls — we need audit logs, token-level cost records, and customer-managed keys for any private deployment.
[08:08] Jesse: Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM and audit logs; our Dedicated also emits request-level tracing and token level cost breakdown in Console. We'll include sample logs and data retention policy in the security pack.

[08:35] Maya: Bench plan? how do we validate that 4 GPUs + 6 burst meets SLO?
[08:40] Anika: We'll run two phases: phase 1 (synthetic micro-bench) to measure per-GPU throughput and latency across prompt lengths. Phase 2 (traffic replay) using your real token distribution and prompt templates to measure p50/p95/p99 end-to-end.

[09:05] Anika: For the traffic replay we need: a) 1 week of anonymized histogram of token lengths, b) 3 representative prompt templates (interactive short, interactive medium, batch long), and c) expected peak concurrency window info.

[09:20] Maya: We'll compile that and share by Monday.

[09:28] Jesse: What about runbook for fallback during spikes? e.g., if pre-warm exhaustion happens, do we automatically pause non-critical batch jobs?
[09:36] Carlos: that would be ideal. night batch should be lower priority.
[09:40] Anika: We can configure priorities at route-level. Batch jobs can be bumped to 'best-effort' when interactive SLOs degrade. Also implement dynamic queuing thresholds with timeouts to avoid unbounded queue growth.

[10:05] Lena: SLA questions — if we use reserved pool + burst, what's the guarantee on burst availability?
[10:12] Jesse: We can offer burst SLAs for POC as part of a paid reserved commitment; typically we commit X amount of burst minutes per month to ensure pre-warmed nodes are available, otherwise fallback rules apply. I'll include sample SLA language.

[10:30] Anika: On cost estimate — reserved GPUs for 6 weeks vs pay-as-you-go: reserved reduces unit cost substantially. For the POC we'll model costs for the proposed 4+2 baseline and 6 burst pre-warm. I'll send a cost sheet with expected token unit economics under different quantization settings.

[11:00] Maya: Bench metrics we'd consider success: interactive p95 < 600ms (short), p95 < 1s (<=600 tokens), p99 < 2s; batch completes nightly jobs within their window (<=4 hours), and cost per 1k tokens below our internal threshold. Also quality: log sample outputs for 200 prompts to spot-check hallucination/regression.

[11:35] Jesse: Good. Anything else on security/compliance?
[11:40] Carlos: We need SOC2 type II evidence and encryption at rest for any logs shared. Also confirm data residency for EU users — not relevant to this POC but may be later.
[11:55] Jesse: We'll attach our security packet and SOC doc. For the bench we'll only need anonymized histograms, not plaintext data.

[12:10] Maya: Timeline recap?
[12:12] Jesse: Reducing to bullets: Redwood provides bench harness by Friday (Anika), customer provides histograms + prompts by Monday (Maya), Redwood runs a 3-day bench mid-June and delivers results + sizing + cost by 2026-06-18. Contract/PO conversation to follow once sizing is validated.

[12:40] Lena: That works. I'm happy to have a short exec readout after bench results.

[13:00] Jesse: Thanks all. we'll follow up with calendar invites and the cost sheet.
[13:06] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[13:08] Carlos: thanks
[13:10] Anika: bye

[13:20] (call end)

Notes on transcription: some technical terms mis-transcribed (e.g., quant vs quantize, Triton sometimes labeled "Trident"), and timestamps approximate.
